300	:ref:`label-theory-shear`, partial differential equations are to be solved
301	with purely Neumann boundary conditions. In the context of the torsion and shear
302	problem, this involves the inversion of a nearly singular global stiffness matrix. After
303	shifting the domain such that the centroid coincides with the global origin, the
304	Lagrangian multiplier method is used to solve the set of linear equations of the form
305	:math:`\textbf{K} \textbf{u} = \textbf{F}` by introducing an extra constraint on the
306	solution vector whereby the mean value is equal to zero. [Larson]_ et al.
307	describe the resulting modified stiffness matrix, and solution and load vector:
308	
309	.. math::
310	  \begin{bmatrix}
311	    \textbf{K} & \textbf{C}^{\rm{T}} \\
312	    \textbf{C} & 0 \\
313	  \end{bmatrix}
314	  \begin{bmatrix}
315	    \textbf{u} \\
316	    \lambda \\
317	  \end{bmatrix} =
318	  \begin{bmatrix}
319	    \textbf{F} \\
320	    0 \\
321	  \end{bmatrix}
322	
323	where :math:`\textbf{C}` is a row vector of ones and :math:`\lambda` may be though of as
324	a force acting to enforce the constraints, which should be relatively small when
325	compared to the values in the force vector and can be omitted from the solution vector.
326	
327	Calculation of Cross-Section Properties
328	---------------------------------------
329	
330	Cross-Sectional Area
331	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
332	
333	The area ``A`` of the cross-section is given by [Pilkey]_:
334	
335	.. math::
336	  A = \int_A dx \, dy = \sum_e A_e = \sum_e \int_{\Omega} J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta
337	
338	As the Jacobian is constant over the element, the integration over the element domain in
339	the above equation can be performed using one point integration:
340	
341	.. math::
342	  A = \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^1 w_i J_i
343	
344	First Moments of Area
345	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
346	
347	The first moments of area are defined by [Pilkey]_:
348	
349	.. math::
350	  Q_x &= \int_A y \, dA = \sum_e \int_{\Omega} \textbf{N} \textbf{y}_e J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta \\
351	  Q_y &= \int_A x \, dA = \sum_e \int_{\Omega} \textbf{N} \textbf{x}_e J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta \\
352	
353	where :math:`\textbf{x}_e` and :math:`\textbf{y}_e` are column vectors containing the
354	cartesian coordinates of the element nodes. The above equations can be evaluated using
355	three point integration as the shape functions (:math:`\textbf{N}`) are quadratic:
356	
357	.. math::
358	  Q_x &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^3 w_i \textbf{N}_i \textbf{y}_e J_e \\
359	  Q_y &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^3 w_i \textbf{N}_i \textbf{x}_e J_e \\
360	
361	Centroids
362	~~~~~~~~~
363	
364	The coordinates of the centroid are found from [Pilkey]_:
365	
366	.. math::
367	  x_c &= \frac{Q_y}{A} \\
368	  y_c &= \frac{Q_x}{A} \\
369	
370	Second Moments of Area
371	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
372	
373	The second moments of area are defined by [Pilkey]_:
374	
375	.. math::
376	  I_{xx} &= \int_A y^2 \, dA = \sum_e \int_{\Omega} (\textbf{N} \textbf{y}_e)^2 J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta \\
377	  I_{yy} &= \int_A x^2 \, dA = \sum_e \int_{\Omega} (\textbf{N} \textbf{x}_e)^2 J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta \\
378	  I_{xy} &= \int_A xy \, dA = \sum_e \int_{\Omega} \textbf{N} \textbf{y}_e \textbf{N} \textbf{x}_e  J_e \, d\eta \, d\xi \, d\zeta \\
379	
380	The above equations can be evaluated using six point integration as the square of the
381	shape functions are quartic:
382	
383	.. math::
384	  I_{xx} &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i (\textbf{N}_i \textbf{y}_e)^2 J_e \\
385	  I_{yy} &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i (\textbf{N}_i \textbf{x}_e)^2 J_e \\
386	  I_{xy} &= \sum_e \sum_{i=1}^6 w_i \textbf{N} \textbf{y}_e \textbf{N} \textbf{x}_e J_e \\
387	
388	The above equations list the second moments of area about the global coordinate system
389	axis, which is chosen arbitrarily by the user. These properties can be found about the
390	centroidal axis of the cross-section by using the parallel axis theorem:
391	
392	.. math::
393	  I_{\overline{xx}} &= I_{xx} - {y_c}^2 A = I_{xx} - \frac{{Q_x}^2}{A} \\
394	  I_{\overline{yy}} &= I_{yy} - {x_c}^2 A = I_{yy} - \frac{{Q_y}^2}{A} \\
395	  I_{\overline{xy}} &= I_{xy} - x_c y_c A = I_{xy} - \frac{Q_x Q_y}{A} \\
396	
397	Radii of Gyration
398	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
399	
400	The radii of gyration can be calculated from the second moments of area and the
401	cross-sectional area as follows [Pilkey]_:
402	
403	.. math::
404	  r_x = \sqrt{\frac{I_{xx}}{A}} \\
405	  r_y = \sqrt{\frac{I_{yy}}{A}} \\
406	
407	.. _label-theory-elastic-section-moduli:
408	
409	Elastic Section Moduli
410	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
411	
412	The elastic section modulii can be calculated from the second moments of area and the
413	extreme (min. and max.) coordinates of the cross-section in the x and y-directions
414	[Pilkey]_:
415	
416	.. math::
417	  Z_{xx}^+ = \frac{I_{\overline{xx}}}{y_{max} - y_c} \\
418	  Z_{xx}^- = \frac{I_{\overline{xx}}}{y_c - y_{min}} \\
419	  Z_{yy}^+ = \frac{I_{\overline{yy}}}{x_{max} - x_c} \\
420	  Z_{yy}^- = \frac{I_{\overline{yy}}}{x_c - x_{min}} \\
421	
422	.. _label-theory-plastic-section-moduli:
423	
424	Plastic Section Moduli
425	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
426	
427	For a homogenous section, the plastic centroid can be determined by finding the
428	intersection of the two lines that evenly divide the cross-sectional area in both the
429	:math:`x` and :math:`y` directions. A suitable procedure could not be found in
430	literature and thus an algorithm involving the iterative incrementation of the plastic
431	centroid was developed. The algorithm uses
432	`Brent's method <https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.optimize.brentq.html>`__
433	to efficiently locate the plastic centroidal axes in the global and principal
434	directions.
435	
436	Once the plastic centroid has been located, the plastic section moduli can be readily
437	computed using the following expression:
438	
439	.. math::
440	  S_{xx} &= \frac{A}{2} \left| y_{c,t} - y_{c,b} \right| \\
441	  S_{yy} &= \frac{A}{2} \left| x_{c,t} - x_{c,b} \right|
442	
443	where :math:`A` is the cross-sectional area, and :math:`x_{c,t}` and :math:`x_{c,b}`
444	refer to the centroids of the top half section and bottom half section respectively.
445	
446	Principal Axis Properties
447	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
448	
449	The principal bending axes are determined by calculating the principal moments of
450	inertia [Pilkey]_:
451	
452	.. math::
453	  I_{11} &= \frac{I_{\overline{xx}} + I_{\overline{yy}}}{2} + \Delta \\
454	  I_{22} &= \frac{I_{\overline{xx}} + I_{\overline{yy}}}{2} - \Delta \\
455	
456	where:
457	
458	.. math::
459	  \Delta = \sqrt{\left(\frac{I_{\overline{xx}} - I_{\overline{yy}}}{2}\right)^2 + {I_{\overline{xy}}}^2}

2	
3	Robbie van Leeuwen and Connor Ferster
4	Independent Researcher, Australia; Independent Researcher, Canada
5	Submitted: 06 November 2023
6	Published: 19 April 2024

9	This is an offline Markdown transcription of the article body and reference list. The

12	
13	## Summary
14	
15	Properties of plane cross-sections are often required in engineering research, analysis,
16	and design. For example, cross-sectional properties are used to determine the
17	displacements, natural frequencies, and stresses within beams under complex loading.
18	`sectionproperties` is a Python package for the analysis of arbitrary cross-sections using
19	the finite element method. `sectionproperties` can be used to determine geometric and
20	warping properties, as well as visualising cross-sectional stresses resulting from
21	combinations of applied loads. `sectionproperties` aims to provide a pre-processor,
22	analysis engine, and post-processor, in a single open source and accessible package, that
23	can be used by researchers, practising engineers, and students.
24	
25	## Statement of Need
26	
27	Obtaining the geometric properties of simple shapes is a classical engineering problem
28	with well-defined analytical solutions. However, obtaining warping properties, for example
29	for torsion and shear analyses, involves solving partial differential equations (Pilkey,
30	2002). While some analytical solutions exist for a small subset of geometries, the method
31	for obtaining these results is not able to be generalised to shapes commonly used in
32	engineering practice. Further, the analysis of arbitrary composite geometries, in which a
33	cross-section could consist of any shape with any number of internal holes, and be made
34	from any number of materials, complicates both geometric and warping computations.
35	
36	To the best of the authors' knowledge, no open source software was available for the
37	computation of both geometric and warping properties for composite, arbitrary
38	cross-sections. Although commercial solutions are available, the article identifies the
39	need for an open-source application programming interface that can be used in research.
40	`sectionproperties` is presented as an open-source solution to arbitrary composite
41	geometric and warping analyses.
42	
43	## Implementation
44	
45	`sectionproperties` uses Shapely (Gillies et al., 2023) for geometry generation and
46	Triangle (Rufat, 2023), a Python port of Triangle (Shewchuk, 2002), to produce a triangular
47	mesh of six-noded quadratic elements. The finite element method is used to solve geometric
48	and warping properties. The latter involves partial differential equations and boundary
49	value problems (Pilkey, 2002).
50	
51	For example, the Saint-Venant torsion constant $J$ is obtained by solving for the warping
52	function $\omega$:
53	
54	$$
55	\nabla^2\omega = 0
56	$$
57	
58	subject to the boundary condition
59	
60	$$
61	\frac{\partial\omega}{\partial x}n_x +
62	\frac{\partial\omega}{\partial y}n_y = y n_x - x n_y.
63	$$
64	
65	Using finite elements, this problem is reduced to a linear system:
66	
67	$$
68	\mathbf{K}\omega = \mathbf{F},
69	$$
70	
71	where the element stiffness matrix and load vector are
72	
73	$$
74	\mathbf{k}^{e} = \sum_{i=1}^{6}w_i\mathbf{B}_i^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{B}_iJ_i,
75	$$
76	
77	$$
78	\mathbf{f}^{e} = \sum_{i=1}^{6}w_i\mathbf{B}_i^\mathsf{T}
79	\begin{bmatrix}
80	\mathbf{N}_i\mathbf{y}_e\\
81	-\mathbf{N}_i\mathbf{x}_e
82	\end{bmatrix}J_i.
83	$$
84	
85	Here $\mathbf{N}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are the shape functions and their derivatives, and
86	$w_i$ and $J_i$ are the integration-point weights and Jacobians. The boundary conditions
87	require inversion of a nearly singular global stiffness matrix. The Lagrangian multiplier
88	method solves the set of equations by introducing a constraint whose mean value is zero:
89	
90	$$
91	\begin{bmatrix}
92	\mathbf{K} & \mathbf{C}^\mathsf{T}\\
93	\mathbf{C} & 0
94	\end{bmatrix}
95	\begin{bmatrix}
96	\mathbf{u}\\
97	\lambda
98	\end{bmatrix}
99	=
100	\begin{bmatrix}
101	\mathbf{F}\\
102	0
103	\end{bmatrix}.
104	$$
105	
106	In this formulation, $\mathbf{C}$ is the assembly of $\sum_i w_i\mathbf{N}_iJ_i$ and
107	$\lambda$ may be treated as a relatively small force that enforces the constraints. Once
108	the warping function has been evaluated, the Saint-Venant torsion constant is
109	
110	$$
111	J = I_{xx} + I_{yy} - \omega^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}\omega.
112	$$
113	
114	The calculation of plastic properties is meshless and is conducted using an iterative
115	method to enforce plastic equilibrium, yielding the plastic centroids. The article directs
116	readers to the documentation for the full theoretical background underpinning
117	`sectionproperties`.
118	
119	![Figure 1: Plot of the centroids and torsion-stress distribution for a bulb section modelled in sectionproperties.](joss_figure_1.png)
120	
121	## Software Development
122	
123	The `sectionproperties` package is distributed as an open-source project. Pre-commit hooks
124	are used to ensure code quality and style consistency across contributions. The project has
125	an extensive testing and validation suite used to verify repeatable output, including a set
126	of benchmarking tests. The project documentation includes installation instructions, a
127	detailed user guide, examples, and an API reference.
128	
129	## Conclusion
130	
131	The authors describe `sectionproperties` as a Python package that calculates section
132	properties of arbitrary sections. They hope it is used by researchers and practising
133	engineers to improve experimental and analysis workflows.

901	Composite Cross-Sections
902	------------------------
903	
904	[Pilkey]_ explains that composite cross-sections can be analysed using a
905	modulus-weighted approach in which the differential area element is multiplied by the
906	elastic modulus for the element, :math:`E_e`:
907	
908	.. math::
909	  d \widetilde{A} = E_e \, dA
910	
911	The expression for section properties after the application of numerical integration
912	then becomes:
913	
914	.. math::
915	  \int f(x,y) \, d \widetilde{A} = \sum_i^n w_i f(\eta_i, \xi_i, \zeta_i) \, J_i E_e
916	
917	[Pilkey]_ also notes that an assumption of the elastic cross-sectional
918	analysis of warping and shear is that:
919	
920	.. math::
921	  \sigma_x = \sigma_y = \tau_{xy} = 0
922	
923	However, for composite sections with variable Poisson's ratios, this assumption does not
924	hold. [Pilkey]_ does mention that engineering materials often have very
925	similar Poisson's ratios and therefore the difference can be negligible.
926	
927	.. note::
928	  If the Poisson's ratio of two materials used in a composite analysis are vastly
929	  different, the assumptions used in ``sectionproperties`` may not hold, see Chapter 5 &

6	Section Object

8	
9	The first step in running a cross-section analysis in ``sectionproperties`` involves the
10	creation of a :class:`~sectionproperties.analysis.section.Section` object. This object
11	stores the cross-section geometry and finite element mesh, providing methods to perform
12	various types of cross-sectional analyses.
13	
14	.. automethod:: sectionproperties.analysis.section.Section.__init__
15	    :noindex:
16	
17	Checking Mesh Quality
18	---------------------
19	
20	Before carrying out a section analysis it is a good idea to check the quality
21	of the finite element mesh. Some useful methods are provided to display mesh statistics
22	and to plot the finite element mesh:
23	
24	..  automethod:: sectionproperties.analysis.section.Section.display_mesh_info
25	    :noindex:
26	
27	..  automethod:: sectionproperties.analysis.section.Section.plot_mesh
28	    :noindex:
29	
30	Geometric Analysis
31	------------------
32	
33	A geometric analysis calculates the area properties of the section.
34	
35	..  automethod:: sectionproperties.analysis.section.Section.calculate_geometric_properties
36	    :noindex:
37	
38	Plastic Analysis
39	----------------
40	
41	A plastic analysis calculates the plastic properties of the section.
42	
43	..  warning:: The plastic analysis in *sectionproperties* assumes all materials are
44	  able to reach their yield stress defined in the material properties. Care should be
45	  taken if analysing materials or cross-sections exhibiting non-linear behaviour, e.g.
46	  reinforced concrete or non-compact steel sections.
47	
48	..  automethod:: sectionproperties.analysis.section.Section.calculate_plastic_properties
49	    :noindex:
50	
51	Warping Analysis
52	----------------
53	
54	A warping analysis calculates the torsion and shear properties of the section.
55	
56	..  warning:: There must be connectivity between all elements of the mesh to perform a
57	  valid warping analysis. This is a limitation of the elastic theory that this
58	  implementation is based on, as there is no way to quantify the transfer of shear and
59	  warping between two unconnected regions.

61	..  automethod:: sectionproperties.analysis.section.Section.calculate_warping_properties

Done. The laboratory reports `post_fix_success` with exit code 0, and all three models report `matches_outline`.

## Root cause

In `source/src/sectionproperties/analysis/section.py`, `calculate_geometric_properties()` and `calculate_frame_properties()` accumulated the **modulus-weighted** first moments (`qx += qx * e`) into `section_props.qx/qy`, which `get_q()` then returned as the documented "first moments of area about the global axis". The weighting is invisible for the default material (`E = 1`) and the centroid/centroidal-post math divided consistently by `ea`, so homogeneous models looked fine — but for any material-bearing model, `get_q()` returned `E·Q`, a physically incompatible ordinary first moment, with no indication.

## Repair (minimal, semantics-preserving)

The theory manual defines `Q_x = ∫_A y dA` as ordinary, and reserves the modulus-weighted convention (Pilkey's `dÃ = E·dA`) for composite *analysis* — which stress recovery, frame properties and the `E.`-prefixed reporting genuinely depend on. So I split the two quantities:

- `section.py` — both geometric and frame analysis now accumulate ordinary `qx/qy` (`+= qx`) and modulus-weighted `eqx/eqy` (`+= qx * e`) on `SectionProperties`; a new `get_eq()` getter exposes the latter; `get_q()` keeps its contract and now returns the true ordinary first moments (docstrings updated).
